Consult Summary:  
45-year-old woman with 3–4 months of progressive soreness, dryness, cracking, and intermittent itching of the skin on her palms and fingers, consistent with irritant contact dermatitis likely related to occupational exposure to cleaning chemicals without protective gloves, exacerbated by underlying type 2 diabetes.

History:  
- Presenting complaint: Soreness, dry cracked skin, and intermittent itching of fingers and palms; skin occasionally bleeds when scratched.  
- Timeline: Symptoms began 3–4 months ago, coinciding with a job change to housekeeping at a hotel; symptoms have worsened to the point of pain and inability to work in the past three days.  
- Exacerbating factors: Frequent exposure to cleaning agents without consistent glove use; working mainly in bathrooms, bedrooms, and corridors.  
- Relieving factors attempted: Over-the-counter use of E45 cream (ineffective), antihistamines (no improvement).  
- Associated symptoms: Mild generalized skin dryness on legs, not severe; no systemic symptoms such as fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary problems; no prior skin conditions reported.  
- Pertinent negatives: No spontaneous bleeding; no rash with vesicles or blisters described; no previous eczema or dermatitis diagnosed.  

Past Medical History:  
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus; no known diabetic complications or neuropathy reported.  
- Denies prior skin disorders including eczema or dermatitis.  

Medications:  
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
- No drug, food, or environmental allergies reported.  

Social History:  
- Occupation: Housekeeper at a hotel, recent job change 4 months ago.  
- Gloves use: Not consistent when handling cleaning chemicals.  
- Smoking: Denies tobacco use.  
- Alcohol: Minimal consumption, approximately a couple of pints per week.  

Family History:  
- Diabetes present in family.  
- No known family history of skin disorders, asthma, or bowel disease.  

Physical Examination:  
- Not recorded in transcript.  

Investigations:  
- None ordered or mentioned.  

Assessment & Plan:  

Overall Impression:  
Irritant contact dermatitis of the hands, likely secondary to chemical exposure from housekeeping duties without adequate hand protection, exacerbated by underlying type 2 diabetes-associated dry skin.  

DDx Integration:  
- Irritant contact dermatitis (high likelihood): Supported by temporal relationship to cleaning chemical exposure, localized hand involvement, and occupational history; no systemic symptoms or rash features opposing diagnosis.  
- Diabetic xerosis with secondary skin changes (medium likelihood): Supported by known diabetes and generalized dryness; opposed by symptom worsening after chemical exposure, suggesting primary irritant cause.  
- Allergic contact dermatitis (medium likelihood): Possible given chemical exposure and itching, but lack of vesicles or response to antihistamines and no allergy history reduce likelihood.  

Issue 1: Irritant Contact Dermatitis  
- Assessment: Likely diagnosis based on chronic occupational exposure, symptom characteristics, and lack of alternative explanations.  
- Plan:  
  • Strongly advise consistent use of protective gloves during all cleaning tasks to avoid irritants.  
  • Prescribe topical corticosteroid cream to reduce inflammation (prescription sent to pharmacy).  
  • Recommend frequent application of stronger emollients (3–4 times daily) for skin hydration over 1–2 weeks.  
  • Advise follow-up if no improvement in 10–14 days or earlier if symptoms worsen, spread, or pain increases.  

Issue 2: Type 2 Diabetes (Relevant as a Comorbidity)  
- Assessment: Diabetes may contribute to skin dryness and impaired healing, potentially exacerbating contact dermatitis.  
- Plan: Continue current management with metformin; monitor skin condition closely. Reinforce diabetic control and skin care education as appropriate.  

General Plan:  
- Safety netting: Patient advised to seek earlier review if symptoms deteriorate or fail to improve with initial treatment.  
- No investigations currently indicated; diagnosis clinical.  

Quality checks:  
- No documented physical exam findings or vital signs.  
- Medication dose and frequency for metformin not documented.  
- No labs or imaging performed.  
- No conflicts between transcript and DDx.  
- Transcript quality clear and audible.
